As I coded that example, before looking at the details, I could talk about some 
that might help. 

The feature that JAGS dose not support but Openbugs does is cycles. 
This happened again in vol3/jama example, in which actually I only writes 
the following now:

# http://www.openbugs.info/Examples/Jama.html
# Jama River Valley Ecuador - Radiocarbon calibration with phase information

# It turns out that the model specified in OpenBUGS
# has *cycles*, which is not support by Stan (and JAGS).
# In section `Directed cycles` of JAGS manual, it writes
#
# Directed cycles are forbidden in JAGS. There are two important instances
# where directed
# cycles are used in BUGS.
# * Defining autoregressive priors
# * Defining ordered priors

So my understanding it that in BUGS, we can specify model, for example, 

## a bi-variate normal for (x1, x2)'
## mu <- c(2, 3); 
## Sigma <- matrix(c(40, 10, 10, 60), ncol = 2) 
## (x1, x2)' ~ mnorm(mu, Sigma) 

model {
  x1 ~ dnorm(mu1, tau1);
  mu1 <- 2 + (x2 - 3) / 6;
  tau1 <- 3 / 115;
  x2 ~ dnorm(mu2, tau2);
  mu2 <- 3 + (x1 - 2) / 4;
  tau2 <- 2 / 115;
}

In Stan, this model would be like 
parameters {
  double x1;
  double x2;
}
model {
   x1 ~ normal(2 + (x2 - 3) / 6, sqrt(115 / 3));
   x2 ~ normal(3 + (x1 - 2) / 4, sqrt(115 / 2)); 
}

However, this would be problematic in Stan as Stan does not check if there is any cycle. 
And this get *directly* translated into a logposterior as 
normal(2 + (x2 - 3) / 6, sqrt(115 / 3)) * normal(3 + (x1 - 2) / 4, sqrt(115 / 2)),
which is not what we want.  

Actually, when we did the Wawro's example, I have noticed that and pointed out that
there are cycles in the model specification.  Back then, I did not how 
stan parse the model.  I am not sure that is a problem. 

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: "cycles" in Stan graphical models (re: BUGS Ice)
parts:
Stan's parser allows cycles. But it's up to you
to make sure the probabilities are correct. For
instance, you can write:

y ~ normal(x,1);
x ~ normal(y,1);

and Stan won't complain. It'll get compiled to

lp__ += normal_log(y,x,1);
lp__ += normal_log(x,y,1);

This is a complete Stan model specifiying joint
probability:

p(x,y) = normal(x|y,1) * normal(y|x,1)

Probably not what we want unless we're hacking an
MI model directly into Stan.

The problem BUGS/JAGS have with cycles conceptually is
that they treat multivariate variable nodes as nodes
of the graph rather than the elements of the vectors.
So if they had:

x[1] ~ normal(0,1);
for (n in 2:N)
x[n] ~ normal(0.5 * x[n-1],1);

They'd think of that as a cycle from x to x because
the variable x shows up on the left-hand and right-hand
sides of the looped sampling.

But the actual random variables are x[1], x[2], ...
and there's no cycle there.

Writing the above kind of thing is totally kosher in
Stan and leads to the right log probability.

- Bob

Stan should be able to handle anything for which you
can:

a. code up the log probability function, and

b. transform all variables to be unconstrained.

Although we don't support undirected graphical models
directly, you can just write out their log probabilities
directly in Stan.

That's what BUGS did in its model. You just need
to be careful you get a proper density (up to a constant).

There are conceptual problems with other BUGS models, like
ordinal logit. To get ordered points c[1] and
c[2], they write something tha also looks circular:

c[1] ~ normal(0,1) I(,c[2]);
c[2] ~ normal(0,1) I(c[1],);

This implies an ill-formed density

p(c) = normal(c[1] | 0, 1) / (1 - pnorm(c[2]|0,1))
* normal(c[2] | 0, 1) / pnorm(c[1]|0,1)

but is OK for sampling using Gibbs as the
conditionals are correct.

What you really need in the model spec
is something like the way you'd write the "same"
thing in Stan:

c[1] ~ normal(0,1)
c[2] ~ normal(0,1) I(c[1],)

This provides a proper density.

BUGS can't handle this version, because there's a chance
you'll sample c[1] from a point above c[2] without
the constraint.

- Bob

I think this is not a correct way of specifying this model. I guess it somehow works in BUGS because they're only ever considering one variable at a time. (Although it seems like you have to exploit some really weird "features" of BUGS to get it to work.) But in general it's by no means true that the joint probability of a bunch of variables is proportional to the product of the conditional probabilities of those variables. For example, the conditional probability of β_1 should be
p(β_1|β_-1) = N(β_1; 2*β_2 - β_3, 1)

and multiplying a bunch of conditionals might

up to a proportion.

messages.subject: improper precision priors; symmetry of mu and y in normal errors
parts: On 1/27/12 8:20 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> I am now pretty sure that the joint prior for the betas is just
> multivariate normal with mean vector zero and a known, very weird,
> precision matrix. So, I would need to implement that, which we had
> talked about before a little bit.

> Do you want a multi_normal_log() whose signature includes a matrix of
> doubles rather than a templated matrix or do you want a function with
> a different name like multi_normal_log_known_precision()?

This is going to lead to an unwieldy profusion of
densities and functions if we're not careful.

We're eventually going to need a multi_normal_log
with a precision matrix instead of covariance matrix
parameter and then there's the full-matrix vs.
Cholesky factor split.

> Also, in
> this case, the precision matrix happens to be singular (thus it's an
> improper prior) so it *can't* allow propto be true;the
> log(det(Sigma)) part would be -Inf. What do you want to do about that?
> I would lean toward making a multi_normal_log_improper() function that
> ignores the constant always.

I think you mean we can't allow propto to be false.
propto=false means include every term in the log
probability function, whereas propto=true includes
only terms containing at least one stan::agrad::var.

The precision matrix will be involved in two terms,
the log(det(Tau)), which we wouldn't evaluate if Tau
was made up of doubles, and the product term with location (mu)
and outcome (y) vectors, which gets evaluated unless the outcome
and both parameters are constant.

What seems to be needed is an "improper" flag
that turns off the check for singularity. But then
there's still the issue of how to pass flags from
Stan to configure the error-checking on a
call-by-call basis.

One way to go would be as Ben suggests, splitting out
the functions, and using names like:

multi_normal_precision_improper_log()

The "_log" needs to go last so that you can refer to
the prefix in stan, as in:

y ~ multi_normal_precision_improper(mu,Tau);

On the other hand, maybe we could add constants to Stan
representing error-checking policies, so that you could
write

y ~ multi_normal_precision(mu,Tau,IMPROPER);

and the IMPROPER would get translated to an error policy
in C++ and passed to the multi_normal_precision function.

But this is problematic in that we only want to turn off
checks for the precision matrix -- we'd still check that
none of the mu or y were NaN and the mu were finite.

Speaking of this latter decision, Matt argued that
outcome y and location mu should be treated symmetrically,
as they're symmetric terms in the probability function.

Boost throws exceptions if mu is infinite when it
constructs a normal_distro(mu,sigma) (Boost doesn't do
multivariate). I thought this made sense, because
a normal_distro(mu,sigma) will always returns 0
probability.

On the other hand, if you have a finite mu and positive
finite sigma, then normal_distro(y|mu,sigma) returns
0. So I also see where Boost's coming from.

The question is, what should we do?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: improper precision priors; symmetry of mu and y in normal errors
parts:
Yes, I meant propto has to (at least in effect) be true when the
precision matrix is singular.

Another possibility for the case where the precision matrix is known
is to precalculate the log determinant, pass it to the function, and
have the function check to see whether it is Inf. In other words, even
if the precision matrix is invertible and the user wants to normalize,
we don't want the function to be recalculating the determinant every
time the function is called anyway.

Relatedly, if the precision matrix is known, I think we would want to
precalculate its 3-factor Cholesky decomposition, Tau = LDL', set U :=
D^(1/2) * L', and pass U rather than Tau. This would save flops inside
the density function, which would basically just be dotself(U.template
triangularView<Eigen::Upper>() * (y - mu)).

So, I don't think we need a version that takes the whole Tau, but the
rest of Bob's questions remain. Also, maybe now is a good time to
reconsider whether we need a CovMatrix class, which could have
attributes like CheckMe, IsPSD, IsPD, IsInverted, LogDeterminant,
CholeskyFactorization, etc. That way the multi_normal_log() functions
could rely more on polymorphing and have the inside of the function
figure out what calculations it needs to do and what calculations it
can avoid by looking at the attributes.

Ben

error checking. For instance, with infinite
degrees of freedom, we want the Student-t
to call the normal. Daniel also pointed out
that the errors need to be checked by the Student-t
so that the error messages make sense to the user.

I've thought about that. We can vectorize the
outcomes and save recalculating inverses and
determinants. But that still does them every
leapfrog step, and it'd be nice to have them
in data. Something like:

data {
cov_matrix(K) Sigma;
}
transformed data {
cov_matrix(K) Tau;
double log_det_Tau;

Tau <- inverse(Sigma);
log_det_Tau <- log(determinant(Tau));
}
model {
for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ multi_normal_prec_det(mu,Tau,log_det_Tau);
}

argument isn't actually log(det(Tau)).

We could also use this exact same strategy
if Sigma were a parameter -- just replace
"data" with "parameters" and "transformed data"
with "transformed parameters". Better yet, use
a local, as in:

parameters {
cov_matrix(K) Sigma;
}
model {
cov_matrix(K) Tau;
double log_det_Tau;

Tau <- inverse(Sigma);
log_det_Tau <- log(determinant(Tau));
for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ multi_normal_prec_det(mu,Tau,log_det_Tau);
}

output as parameters as they would be if declared
as "transformed parameters".

in the data.

I'll have to think more about this.

I've been designing everything with a much more
functional than object orientation. It's much
simpler conceptually as there's no pre-conditions
or post-conditions in an object's state to maintain.

So I've been thinking much more of this kind of
optimization work would be done by rewriting the grammars,
which I have to admit, is far from ideal for readability.

I don't see how to maintain these states given
the flexibility of Eigen matrice's operator[],
which returns a REFERNENCE to an element:

Matrix<T,...>

If someone gets such a reference and changes it,

In the CovMatrix class in my head, there would be constructors that

should subsequently be changing its elements before the posterior is
evaluated. I might even overload [] and () to throw errors. But if

Maybe I haven't emphasized the following enough:

-- There are a small number of ways to construct a covariance matrix
that guarantee it will be positive definite
-- And there are a great many ways of constructing a covariance matrix
that do not have a snowball's chance in hell of being positive
definite in all 1000 (or even 3) iterations. The subset of positive
definite matrices within the set of symmetric matrices with positive
diagonal elements is just too small.

So, although we probably can't absolutely prevent the following from
happening:

parameters {
double covariances[K * (K - 1) / 2 + K];
}
transformed parameters {
double Sigma[K,K];
int count;

count <- 1;
for (i in 1:K) {
for (j in i:K) {
Sigma[i,j] <- covariances[count];
Sigma[j,i] <- Sigma[i,j]
count <- count + 1;
}
}

because Sigma will not be positive definite in the vast majority of
the iterations. Users should be using convenience functions in
their .stan files like makeLKJ(), makeAR1(), etc. that output valid

way of indicating that the density should not check Sigma.

way of constructing a positive definite covariance matrix that a user
wants to use but isn't implemented in Stan. In that case, they would
have to do it themselves within the .stan file. But I would almost
rather them email a feature request.

I do kind of like the design of the Matrix package in R (as opposed to
the matrix that is in the base R package, which is basically just a
vector of numbers with a dimensions attribute). You can see its design
for a correlation matrix, for example, with

library(Matrix)
help("corMatrix-class")

A corMatrix has a slot (attribute) called "factors", which is a list
that caches any matrix factorizations like Cholesky and so forth. So
when some high-level operation (like det()) is done to a corMatrix,
the low-level internals are free to carry that out via the Cholesky
factor.

Ben

Because you have to do the same solve N times.
An alternative is to vectorize, and write:

y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);

for vector y. Then multi_normal_log does the same unfolding
inside its loop. If the mu are determined by regressions,
then we also need to allow passing in a sequence of mu
vectors.

y[n] ~ normal(alpha + beta * x[n], sigma);

with alpha, beta and x[n] simple scalars, turns into

y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma);

where y is a vector, x is a vector and alpha and
beta are still scalars, with the expression defined so that

(alpha + beta * x)[n]
= alpha + beta * x[n].

so that the whole is equivalent to the original statement
looping over the N.

So far, we've only done this for the regular normal,
and even then, we haven't allowed varying means. It'll
be a much bigger saving with covariance matrices.

>> Are you suggesting we extend Eigen with a CovMatrix class?
>
> Maybe. I think eventually Eigen will probably extend itself with all
> kinds of structured matrices, but that is not on their agenda right
> now.

Doug Bates and some other folks have been pushing
things like symmetric matrix and easier handling
of positive definiteness

> So, we could "extend" Eigen's Matrix class (and possibly deal

> or we could make a totally new class called CovMatrix that "embeds"
> one or more Eigen Matrices as private attributes so that Stan can
> pretty much keep the same API even if Eigen changes in major ways.

I was thinking of whether we'd just do something
in Stan's compiled language, whether we'd try to
do something with a nice C++ API to build into our
matrix class, or whether we'd just do something with
Stan's own modeling language.

Either way, it makes sense to me to extend Matrix.
After all, a CovMatrix is a Matrix. That lets us apply
all of the usual operators to it. But given C++'s semantics,
that'd really want us to allow the assignment and
access referent operators. If it doesn't extend Matrix,
we'll have a ton of work to do defining all the operators
for it. But then maybe it won't have many.

These kinds of extensions seem to be on Eigen's agenda,
just not highly prioritized. They're willing to help
with high-level design advice, but need someone to code
and test.

We already plan to go down this road in the near future.
Eigen needs someone to push through all the heterogeneous
operator traits (so that you could multiply a Matrix<var,...>
and a Matrix<double,...>). That's what we need for much more
efficient matrix auto-diff operations. Right now, we're
coding around their expressions and have to over-promote
doubles to auto-dif variables, which is costly in terms of
both time and memory.

Currently, Eigen has an example for Matrix<complex,...> and
Matrix<double,...>, but it's hard coded for those types.
That opens the way to an intermediate possibility where we
just follow what they did for complex rather than trying to
generalize all their matrix and operator traits.

- Bob

Aha! Now I see. Yes, we should definitely avoid recalculating an
inverse or a determinant. And, we should try to avoid making users
write optimized .stan files. Ideally, they should just write readable
(and correct) .stan files and Stan should figure out how to do it
fast.

With covariance matrices (more so than other parameters), numerical
algorithms need "the" covariance matrix in various forms. Sometimes
--- but rarely --- you need the literal, textbookish, KxK form,
sometimes you need the SelfAdjointView, sometimes you need a
correlation matrix and standard deviations, sometimes you need a
Cholesky factor, sometimes you need the inverse, etc. And on top of
that, you don't want to store more than you need or being doing the
same autodiff twice, so you have various storeage schemes, dense vs.
sparse, etc. All of that would seem to argue for making a CovMatrix
class (extending Matrix is fine with me) that is capable of
implementing all this but mostly hides the implementation.

Since Doug already went down this road for the Matrix library in R,
I'm sure we could coordinate with him on how best to do it with Eigen.

Ben
